paragraphs.heading: What a hot Jupiter is
paragraphs.text: A hot Jupiter is a gas giant planet around another star that seems to be built much like Jupiter, yet goes around its star in less than ten days. Lighter ones are sometimes called hot Saturns. The nickname comes from two things: these planets sit very close to their stars, and their atmospheres are very hot. Their masses run from about 0.36 to 11.8 times that of Jupiter.

paragraphs.heading: Easy to spot
paragraphs.text: Of all planets beyond our Solar System, hot Jupiters are the easiest to find with the radial-velocity method, which looks for the wobble a planet causes in its star's motion. A hot Jupiter makes its star sway in larger and quicker movements than other known kinds of planets do. One well-known example is 51 Pegasi b. Found in 1995, it was the first planet discovered around a star like the Sun, and it circles its star in about four days.

paragraphs.heading: Round orbits, one face to the star
paragraphs.text: Most hot Jupiters follow nearly circular paths. Astronomers think tugs from nearby stars, or tidal forces, rounded those orbits out. Whether a planet keeps such an orbit for a long time or ends up crashing into its star depends on how its orbit and its body change together, linked by tidal stretching and lost energy. Usually one side of the planet always faces the star, a state called tidal locking.

paragraphs.heading: Puffed up
paragraphs.text: Many of these planets have strangely low densities. The lowest measured so far belongs to TrES-4b, at 0.222 g/cm³. Why they are so large is not yet fully understood. Suggested reasons include strong light from the star, atmospheres that light has trouble passing through, possible energy sources inside the planet, and orbits so tight that the outer layers get pulled further outward.

paragraphs.heading: Wild weather
paragraphs.text: Short years, long days and tidal locking probably give hot Jupiters extreme and unusual atmospheres. Models predict fierce winds, jet streams racing around the equator, and storms that stir hot and cold gas together. For a model based on the planet HD 209458 b, the day side comes out about 500 K hotter than the night side.

paragraphs.heading: Which stars have them
paragraphs.text: Hot Jupiters seem to turn up more often around F- and G-type stars, less often around K-type stars, and very rarely around red dwarfs. Any such pattern has to allow for biases in how planets get observed. Even so, their numbers drop off exponentially when set against the star's absolute magnitude.

paragraphs.heading: How did they get there
paragraphs.text: Astronomers have three schools of thought about where hot Jupiters come from. One says they formed right where we see them. Another says they formed farther out, beyond the frost line, from rock, ice and gas, and later moved inward until they settled into a stable orbit. That move might have been driven by gas and dust while the young star still had its nebula, or by a close pass of another large body that unsettled the planet's orbit.

paragraphs.heading: Grown from a super-Earth
paragraphs.text: A different idea starts with a super-Earth, a more common kind of planet, as the core. That core would have gathered its thick gas envelope at its present distance, turning into a gas giant on the spot. Because super-Earths often have companion planets, hot Jupiters made this way would be expected to have companions too.
